text:
I spent part of this week thinking about pipes and handshakes.

That is an odd way to describe two pieces of African infrastructure research. But both papers my team published this week ask much the same question: when a market is moving quickly, which connections need to be designed before today’s sensible choices become tomorrow’s expensive constraints?

In Rwanda, the answer may literally be a pipe between two factories. The country is looking at industrial symbiosis: one firm’s waste heat, water or by-products becoming another firm’s useful input. Financially, shared systems can cut energy, treatment and logistics costs and make industrial parks more competitive. Ethically, public and development capital should create durable productive value, not just a collection of green-looking features.

The difficult bit is coordination. UNIDO found hundreds of potential symbiosis opportunities across industrial parks, but far fewer had become operating assets. My team’s conclusion is that the missing ingredient is often not technology. It is the boring but essential machinery of contracts, standards, park management, finance and trust.

Read the Rwanda research:
https://stonecomms.com/research/pipe-between-factories-africa-eco-industrial-parks

Kenya’s electric-motorcycle market presents the same problem in another form. Battery swapping is scaling fast. Several networks can each work well on their own and still leave riders, investors and utilities with a fragmented system later.

Our recommendation is deliberately narrow: standardise the handshake, not the whole machine. Keep the interfaces that matter — access, payment, safety data, electrical and physical connections, governance — contestable before capital and customer habits harden around incompatible networks. Financially, that protects competition and reduces stranded-infrastructure risk. Ethically, riders should not bear the cost of avoidable lock-in created upstream.

Read the Kenya research:
https://stonecomms.com/research/open-before-it-locks-kenya-battery-swapping-interoperability

Next week my team is looking at two more questions worth watching: whether Africa’s clean-cooking gains are becoming too dependent on fragile fuel supply chains, and whether gender-lens finance is solving the risk problem faster than it is making viable women-owned businesses visible to lenders.
